title: Why bacterial percentages can hide what roots experience
lesson_title: Why bacterial percentages can hide what roots experience
topic: Plant–soil microbiome dynamics and nutrient interactions
summary: How decades of fertilizer management and changing plant age shape soybean root bacteria, why microbial amounts differ from percentages, and what small-community growth tests can and cannot prove.
paper_title: Dynamic root microbiome sustains soybean productivity under unbalanced fertilization

vocabulary.definition: A community of microorganisms associated with a particular environment.
vocabulary.example: The root microbiome changed as soybean plants developed.

vocabulary.definition: The soil closely influenced by roots.
vocabulary.example: Bacterial loads fell in the phosphorus-limited rhizosphere.
The root endosphere differed from the surrounding soil.
The team sampled plants after germination.

vocabulary.definition: A small root structure that can contain nitrogen-fixing partner bacteria.
vocabulary.example: Soybean formed more nodules in the treatment without nitrogen fertilizer.

vocabulary.definition: Converting nitrogen from the air into forms that organisms can use.
vocabulary.example: Nitrogen fixation helps support the soybean partnership.

vocabulary.definition: A group’s share of the total community.
vocabulary.example: Relative abundance can fall while the amount of a group increases.

vocabulary.definition: An estimate of how much of a group is present, rather than its percentage.
vocabulary.example: Absolute abundance increased despite a falling percentage.

vocabulary.definition: The estimated amount of microorganisms present in a sample.
vocabulary.example: Microbial load was measured using DNA reference sequences.

vocabulary.definition: More strongly represented in a comparison.
vocabulary.example: Phosphorus-related genes were enriched under phosphorus limitation.

vocabulary.definition: A small community assembled deliberately from selected microorganisms.
vocabulary.example: The synthetic community contained five bacterial strains.

vocabulary.definition: The material in which an organism grows.
vocabulary.example: The controlled experiment used vermiculite as its substrate.

scope_note: Soybean study at one long-term field site plus short seedling experiments in sterilized vermiculite. No claim of sorghum nodulation, field-yield improvement from SynCom inoculation, direct conversion from DNA abundance to nutrient flux, or detected nitrogen fixation by the tested SynCom strains.
attribution: Original educational narration adapted from Wang et al., Nature Communications 15, 1668 (2024), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45925-5. The original article is licensed CC BY 4.0. This lesson simplifies and reorganizes the findings and adds clearly identified teaching examples, limitations, and proposed applications; it is not the original article text.
narration_notes: Continuous original English narration, no exercises. The simple 100/200-unit community example is explicitly hypothetical. Statistical non-significance, gene-copy measurement limits, and sorghum/model extrapolation are explained in the spoken script.
